adds.title: Proceedings and Judgments in the Safiyatu Hussaini Case (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. V)
adds.summary: This chapter of the academic sourcebook reproduces the full record of a capital prosecution in Sokoto State's Sharia courts. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa (Sokoto State) convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. On her appeal, filed 26 October 2001, the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. For this record the document evidences that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the same capital-punishment framework (for zina, not same-sex conduct) the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

adds.title: Interim and Final Reports of the Committee Set Up to Advise the Sokoto State Government on the Establishment of Sharia (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. II)
adds.summary: Primary committee reports mapping Sokoto's Sharia adoption: the interim report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999 and the final report on 16 December 1999, with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in Sokoto State. They document the state-level groundwork for the Sokoto Sharia Penal Code - in force from 31 January 2001 per this record's other sources - that carries the stoning and lashing penalties for men's same-sex acts described in this record.

adds.title: Yobe State - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Reference article on Yobe State recording that the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims and that Sharia law was established in the state in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim. For this record it confirms, in a jurisdiction-specific source, that Yobe adopted Sharia within the 1999-2002 wave that created the state's parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims.

adds.title: On the Adoption and Implementation of Sharia Legal System in Zamfara State (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. II)
adds.summary: Primary state-authored account of Zamfara's Sharia adoption, written by Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, and presented at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. It details Zamfara's enabling legislation - the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999 under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution - which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code, and records the Grand Kadi taking over court administration from 29 June 2000 alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. For this record it documents from inside the state government the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

adds.title: The Making of the Zamfara and Kano State Sharia Penal Codes (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. IV)
adds.summary: Academic reconstruction of how Zamfara's Sharia Penal Code was made: the Zamfara governor appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementing Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, and by the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia. The chapter analyses the codification of offences and punishments and the penal-code architecture the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, grounding this record's claim that Zamfara pioneered the bloc's religious-criminal framework.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Malaysia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: The page's dedicated Kedah section reports the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014): liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex) are criminalised under sections 23 and 24, punishable by up to RM5,000 fine, up to 3 years' imprisonment, or up to 6 strokes of whipping (or any combination); a male posing as a woman in public is criminalised under section 26 (up to RM1,000 fine or up to 1 year imprisonment), while female cross-dressing is not; women convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to 6 months under section 52. For this record: Kedah-specific state criminal law covering same-sex conduct and trans male-to-female public presentation, the direct legal risk a trans visitor faces in this state.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), and the page names Papua among the provinces whose trans residents have benefited (with Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung); only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same page's national-framework facts apply in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage (up to one year in prison) takes effect on 2 January 2026, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and customary laws may apply. For this record: evidence that trans people in Papua may obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme, and the national legal framework a trans visitor stands under while in the province.
